prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Checkers on an 8x8 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(my_men, my_kings, opp_men, opp_kings, color) -> tuple[tuple[int, int], tuple[int, int]]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `my_men` is a list of squares containing your regular pieces. - `my_kings` is a list of squares containing your kings. - `opp_men` is a list of squares containing opponent regular pieces. - `opp_kings` is a list of squares containing opponent kings. - `color` is your color: `'b'` for black which moves downwards (to lower row values) and `'w'` for white which moves upwards (to higher row values). - Squares use coordinates: row `0`-`7`, column `0`-`7`. - `(0, 0)` is the bottom-left corner; rows increase bottom-to-top and columns increase left-to-right. - Only dark squares are playable. # Action / Return Format - Return a move as a tuple: `((from_row, from_col), (to_row, to_col))`. - `from_row`, `to_row`, `from_col`, `to_col` are coordinates `0..7`. - (`from_row`, `from_col`) has to be a coordinate of a piece that is yours and (`to_row`, `to_col`) has to be the destination square.Return a legal move; captures are mandatory when available. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm sketching out a checkers AI using alpha-beta pruning, starting with the core rules: black moves down the board, white moves up, regular pieces move diagonally forward while kings can move any diagonal direction, and captures are mandatory. I need to clarify whether multi-jump sequences are required in this implementation.

Looking at the move format constraint—just a single (from, to) tuple per call—I'm thinking through whether the arena expects each jump step individually or the complete multi-jump path. The safest bet is to assume each function call handles one move or one jump step, and if a piece can continue jumping, the game will call the policy again with the updated board state. This way I can compute all possible legal moves and prioritize captures appropriately.

Building the move generator now... I'm restructuring the move generation to use a unified representation where each side has explicit character codes for men and kings, plus a forward direction parameter. This way I can handle both my pieces and opponent pieces with the same logic. Now I'm working on the recursive jump-finding function that will explore all possible capture sequences from a given position. Refactoring the jump logic to be cleaner—I'll represent each move as a path of squares plus the set of captured pieces, then use recursion to explore all possible jump sequences from each landing position.

Now I'm thinking through the evaluation function: pieces are worth around 100 for men and 160 for kings, with positional bonuses for advancement, center control, and back-row defense. For the minimax search with alpha-beta pruning, depth 6-8 should be manageable with decent move ordering. The tricky part is how to return multi-jump moves—the arena likely expects a single move tuple from start to final position, so I'll need to flatten the full jump sequence into that format.

Actually, I'm reconsidering: if the arena expects step-by-step moves and calls back for mandatory captures, I should just return the first step of any multi-jump sequence. That way the search treats a full capture chain as one ply, but the actual move returned is just the initial step. The arena will handle the continuation.

Building the policy function now...

Implementing the alphabeta search with iterative deepening and a time budget... Implementing the move generation logic... I'm realizing the logic for landing squares needs clarification — a piece can only land on empty squares, which are either originally empty or the starting position (since the piece moved from there). The captured opponent pieces stay on the board during the chain since in American checkers they're only removed after the complete move finishes, but we track them separately to prevent jumping the same piece twice. I'm verifying the landing logic handles all the edge cases correctly—when we land at start_pos, it's actually occupied in the original board, so the condition `land in board and land != start_pos` correctly allows it, and previous intermediate squares are empty so they don't cause issues either.

Now I'm writing an evaluation function that scores positions based on piece advancement, center control, and piece values, with kings weighted higher than regular pieces and opponent pieces penalized symmetrically.

I need to handle the endgame cases where one side runs out of moves or pieces—the alphabeta pruning already catches those by returning extreme scores. For efficiency, I'm sticking with dictionaries for the board representation since the search depth should stay manageable within the time limit, and I'll rely on move ordering (captures first) to help with pruning.

Setting up the main policy function... I'm implementing the move generation logic, checking for valid jumps recursively and handling king promotions when pieces reach the back row.

Implementing game tree search... Finishing the opponent's piece evaluation with center distance, then returning the total score. I'm realizing there's a potential bug in my iterative deepening where I check time constraints but might not complete iterations cleanly, so I should just let it run and handle timeouts instead. Also, if there's only one legal move available, I can skip the search entirely. The bigger question is how the arena handles multi-jump sequences—whether it calls my policy function for each sub-jump or expects the complete move in one call. Given that uncertainty, I'm leaning toward returning just the first step of a multi-jump, assuming the arena will call me again for continuation, though this could be risky if it expects the full (start, end) encoding that many checkers APIs use. I need to make a decision here about what format to return. I'm leaning toward returning just the first step of any multi-jump sequence to be safe, since the arena likely calls repeatedly if more jumps are available. For the search strategy, I need to balance depth with performance—depth 6 with ~8 moves per position gets expensive fast, so I'll aim for depth 4-5 and focus on move ordering to improve pruning efficiency.

Writing the policy function... I'm working through the logic of move validation and promotion rules. In American checkers, men promote only at the end of a move, and kings are short-range (one square diagonally), not flying kings. During multi-jump sequences, if a man becomes king mid-jump, it stops jumping immediately rather than continuing—my find_jumps function handles this by adding the move to results and not recursing further. I'm also confirming that whether a move is a regular step or a capture, the first step is always represented as (path[0], path[1]), and promotion happens correctly when a man reaches the king row. Ready to write the final implementation.
